questions.question: How should you type a component's props today?
options: By annotating the props parameter directly
By typing the return value only
questions.explanation: `React.FC` no longer adds children in React 18 types and complicates generic components. Annotating the parameter is the current recommendation.

questions.question: Which type covers anything React can render?
questions.explanation: `ReactNode` includes elements, strings, numbers, arrays, null and undefined. `ReactElement` is only a single element.

questions.question: How do you make a wrapper accept every prop the underlying button accepts?
questions.explanation: `ComponentProps<"button">` pulls in the full set of typed button attributes, so onClick, disabled and aria attributes all work.

questions.question: What is wrong with useState([])?
options: TypeScript infers never[], so nothing can be added to the array
It infers any[], removing type safety
questions.explanation: An empty array literal gives `never[]`. Supply the element type: `useState<Item[]>([])`.

questions.question: Why type a context as AuthValue | null and guard it in a hook?
options: The guard both catches a missing provider at runtime and narrows the type for every caller
null is the only valid default
questions.explanation: The runtime check throws when the provider is missing, and TypeScript narrows the return type so callers never handle null.

questions.question: Which type describes a change event on a text input?
Why prefer currentTarget over target in a typed handler?
options: currentTarget is typed as the element the handler is attached to, while target is the more general EventTarget
questions.explanation: `target` can be any descendant, so its type is broad and usually forces a cast. `currentTarget` is precisely typed.

questions.question: Why prefer a status union over separate boolean flags?
options: A union makes impossible combinations such as loading and error at once unrepresentable
Booleans cannot be used in state
Unions are required by strict mode
questions.explanation: Two booleans allow four states, only three of which are valid. A union closes the set so invalid states cannot be written.
